slides.title: The ten-million-token question
slides.caption: Memory systems are scored on conversations that fit in an email thread. The work an enterprise wants remembered is years of mail, chat, tickets and documents.

slides.title: What we will cover
slides.caption: How large the workload is, in tokens. What the one public test at ten million shows. What the vendors report. Why ten million is hard. The question, left open.

slides.title: One worker, one year
slides.caption: Microsoft counts 117 emails and 153 chat messages received per weekday. At 144 words per email, that is about 6 to 8 million tokens a year, derived.

slides.title: Sourced anchors for scale
slides.caption: One company's senior mail from the 2000s is about 100 million tokens. A mailbox quota is 100 gigabytes. All US annual reports since 1993 are 6.5 billion tokens.

slides.title: The one public test at ten million
slides.caption: BEAM has one hundred synthetic conversations, ten of them at ten million tokens, and two thousand questions across ten abilities. A judge scores each answer 0, 0.5 or 1.

slides.title: What the test shows
slides.caption: With a one-million-token model, full context scores 0.10 at ten million, retrieval 0.25, and the authors' memory design 0.27. Scores are low at every length.

slides.title: What the vendors report
slides.caption: Three vendors published their own ten-million-token numbers. Each used its own judge and harness. None is comparable to the paper, and none has been reproduced.

slides.title: Two independent points beside them
slides.caption: A 2026 corpus benchmark reports a memory agent at 11.1 and retrieval at 1.2 over ten million tokens. A 115-million-token benchmark reports a file-storing agent at 72.5.

slides.title: Why ten million is hard
slides.caption: Nothing can read the whole. The candidate pool is too dense for an encoder. And the evidence is spread across years. The three compound.

slides.title: At that density, words discriminate
slides.caption: On the ten-million-token benchmark, exact word overlap between question and evidence predicts whether the evidence is found. The choice of encoder does not.

slides.title: Question one: which architecture
slides.caption: Which architecture, if any, gives an agent useful recall over ten million tokens of its own records? And at a cost a service desk can bear?

slides.title: Question two: how would you know
slides.caption: The score would have to be independently produced, on a corpus that does not fit a context window. Unit, pool, k and judge stated. Two separate tables.

slides.title: Question three: what would it cost
slides.caption: What would it cost to index? Sending everything to the model costs one to six hundred dollars per ten million tokens. How do the two compare?

slides.title: What to remember
slides.caption: Ten million tokens is one worker's year, and the floor. The best independent result there is 0.27. Vendor numbers are unchecked. The question is open.
